analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal corporate income tax rate to roughly 10–20%, tied to foreign averages.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on February 10, 2016 and died there when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the federal corporate income tax rate from 35% to whichever is greater: 10%, or five points below the average corporate rate of other developed (OECD) countries. It also requires Congress to approve any future rate increases with a new law, while automatic cuts take effect on their own. It never received a hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders. Cutting the rate from 35% to the 10–20% range would reduce what profitable companies owe the Treasury by a large share, which flows through mainly to shareholders, who are disproportionately higher-income households. The bill's sponsors argued a lower rate would also encourage companies to invest and hire in the United States instead of locating profits abroad.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the corporate rate at the greater of 10% or five percentage points below the average corporate tax rate of OECD countries other than the United States, replacing the 35% rate for tax years beginning after December 31, 2016 [S2][S3].
The Treasury Secretary must recalculate the OECD-based rate every five years, and the bill updates related withholding and corporate-inversion rules to use the new rate [S3].

If the recalculated rate would be higher than the prior year's, it takes effect only if Congress passes a joint resolution approving it within 60 days; otherwise the lower prior rate stays in place [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury, and ultimately taxpayers, lose the revenue the higher corporate rate collected — most of it paid by profitable corporations. Under the bill, any future increase in the corporate rate requires new legislation, while cuts happen automatically, making revenue harder to restore later. Supporters argue lower rates would pay back some of this through growth; the bill itself contains no offsetting revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts the corporate rate with no offsetting revenue, so it directly reduces federal receipts and would add to deficits unless other taxes rose or spending fell [S2][S3].
Corporate tax savings accrue primarily to shareholders, who are concentrated among wealthier households, so the tax cut's direct benefit skews toward higher-income Americans.

The procedure is asymmetric: automatic cuts take effect on their own, but any increase requires Congress to enact a joint resolution within 60 days, structurally biasing the rate downward over time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost is clear: a large, uncompensated reduction in federal revenue at a time when the rate stood at 35%, with benefits flowing disproportionately to shareholders. The claimed upside — more investment and jobs at lower rates — was the sponsors' argument, but the bill contains no test or guarantee of that outcome. The one-sided adjustment mechanism makes it easier to cut the rate than to raise it, even if future fiscal conditions call for more revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Emmer introduced the bill on February 10, 2016, joined by three Republican cosponsors (Reps. Love, Mulvaney, and Williams) [S3][S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the action history shows no further action of any kind [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired in committee without a hearing or a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and shareholders are better off because the bill died — the 35% corporate rate stayed in place for the rest of the Congress rather than dropping to the 10–20% range. Federal revenue was not cut; taxpayers and beneficiaries of federally funded programs are spared the revenue loss, though supporters of the bill would say the economy lost the investment they believed lower rates would attract.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations kept the 35% rate they pay

for.name: Rep. Tom Emmer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the corporate rate to the OECD average [S3][S4].

for.name: Reps. Mia Love, Mick Mulvaney, and Roger Williams

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans, and the bill received no Democratic cosponsors [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have cut the 35% rate to the greater of 10% or five points below the OECD average, sharply reducing corporate tax bills. Because it never advanced, corporations continue paying the 35% rate, so its failure preserves their tax burden.
Corporate tax cuts flow mostly to shareholders, who are concentrated among wealthier households. The bill's death means they did not receive the after-tax gain it would have delivered.
